1.x: The “householder” represents God (the Father, YHWH, the Holy Spirit, the divine Spirit of Jesus, all of which are the same divine Spirit, not multiple divine persons like Trinitarians teach), and the “vineyard” is His Kingdom or work on Earth.

2.x: The first group of workers makes a specific legal contract with the master: they agree to work the whole 12-hour day for a “penny” (a Roman denarius), which was the standard, perfectly fair daily wage for a laborer at the time. This represents people who enter a relationship with God based on law, merit, or a calculation of what they expect to earn.

3.x: The householder returns to the marketplace at the “third hour” (9:00 AM).

4.x: Notice the shift in the agreement. There is no longer a negotiated contract for a set amount. The master simply says: “whatsoever is right I will give you.” These workers go into the vineyard entirely trusting the master’s character and justice, rather than a specific legal guarantee.

5.x: The householder returns to the marketplace at the “sixth hour” (noon) and the “ninth hour” (3:00PM).

6.x: The “eleventh hour” is 5:00PM. With only a single hour left of daylight before the workday ends (since in biblical times the working day began at 6:00AM and went for 12 hours).

7.x: When asked why they are doing nothing, they explain it isn’t out of laziness, but because no one gave them an opportunity. Spiritually, this points to those who are called late in life, or groups historically left out (like the Gentiles compared to Israel). They are given the same promise: trust the master, and he will pay what is right.

8.x: According to OT Law (“the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning”, Lev 19:13 KJV), poor laborers had to be paid at the end of every single day. The master intentionally tells his steward to pay the workers in reverse order, starting with those who only worked one hour.

9.x: The workers that only worked for one hour receive the same penny that the early workers had agreed for.

10.x: When the one-hour workers receive a full day’s wage (a penny), the 12-hour workers naturally assume their pay will scale up proportionally. They expect a bonus based on human logic. Instead, they receive exactly the same single penny they legally shook hands on.

11.x: The early workers complain (“murmured”) to the “goodman” (the master).

12.x: Their grievance feels completely logical to human standards of fairness: “We sweated out here in the blistering midday sun, and you made these guys equal to us?” This exposes the heart of religious entitlement. They didn’t actually lose anything they were promised; they are just upset that others received unconditional grace. In a spiritual sense, this warns long-time believers or religious elites against resenting God’s radical mercy toward deathbed converts or notorious sinners.

16.x: Jesus repeats the phrase he used back in Mt 19:30. In the kingdom of heaven, status is completely flipped. Those who think their long tenure, hard labor, or personal righteousness makes them “first” in God’s eyes will find themselves at the back of the line if they lack love and humility. Meanwhile, those who come to God with nothing to offer but humility (the “last”), they are elevated by His grace.

17.x: Jesus is traveling “up” to Jerusalem, both geographically (Jerusalem is up in the mountains) and spiritually, toward the ultimate climax of his earthly ministry. The roads would have been packed with crowds of pilgrims heading to the city for Passover. Because of the noise and the crowds, Jesus deliberately pulls the twelve core disciples “apart” (aside) along the road to share something private. This was confidential Kingdom business. The public wasn’t ready to handle what was coming, and honestly, neither were the disciples. Jesus wanted to prepare his closest followers so that when the nightmare of the crucifixion unfolded, they would eventually remember he was in complete control the entire time.

18.x: Notice how specific this is. He doesn’t just say: “Things are going to get rough.” He explicitly states he will be betrayed (pointing directly to Judas Iscariot’s upcoming actions) and handed over to the Jewish religious authorities (the chief priests and scribes). Under Jewish Law, the Sanhedrin (the high council) would formally pronounce a death sentence on him for blasphemy, even though they lacked the legal authority under Roman occupation to actually execute anyone.

19.x: Because the Jewish leaders couldn’t legally execute Jesus, they had to “deliver him to the Gentiles” - meaning the Roman authorities (specifically Pontius Pilate). Jesus then names the exact sequence of Roman punishment: mocking, scourging (whipping), and crucifixion. He ends with the ultimate promise: rising on the third day. This verse displays Jesus’ divine foreknowledge. The human does not know all things (Mt 24:36), but the Father, dwelling in Jesus, reveals to the human what he needs to know: "For all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you" (Jn 14:10 KJV); "The Revelation of Jesus Christ(the Son), which God(the Father) gave unto him..." (Rev 1:1 KJV); and "For the Father loveth the Son, and sheweth him all things that himself doeth..." (Jn 5:20 KJV). In the ancient world, “Gentiles” and “crucifixion” went hand-in-hand, as crucifixion was a uniquely brutal Roman method of execution reserved for slaves and rebels. Jesus foretells the exact physical trauma he will endure: (1) “to mock”: Roman soldiers putting a crown of thorns on him and a purple robe; (2) “to scourge”: the brutal whipping with a cat-o’-nine-tails that often killed men before they even reached the cross; (3) “to crucify”: the literal nailing to the wood. But Jesus doesn’t leave them in the grave. The verse ends with the ultimate pivot of the Christian faith: “and the third day he shall rise again.” The horror of the execution is entirely eclipsed by the triumph of the resurrection.

20.x: The mother of Zebedee’s children (historically identified as Salome, who was most likely the sister of Jesus’ mother, Mary. You can see this by comparing these parallel passages: Mt 27:56; Mark 15:40; & Jn 19:25) approaches Jesus with James(the Great) and John(the beloved disciple, author of John), Jesus’ cousins. She kneels in a posture of deep respect (“worshipping him”), but she is there to negotiate a favor. Mark 10:35 says James and John themselves raised the question of v.21. There is no contradiction. It is possible either that the three of them asked together, or perhaps even more likely that they had discussed it among themselves beforehand, and each posed the question to Jesus privately.

21.x: Salome’s petition was likely inspired by Jesus’s remarks in 19:28, where he had announced the Twelve’s rulership with him in his future kingdom. She asks for the two absolute highest positions of honor and authority in Christ’s future kingdom - the seats directly to his right and left. Despite Jesus just explaining that his path leads to execution, the disciples are still thinking in terms of an earthly political coup. They assume Jesus is about to overthrow the Romans and set up a physical government. James and John use their mother to make the request, likely hoping Jesus’ familial affection would make it harder for him to say no. This in-fighting for the highest position was a recurring matter among the disciples (Mt 18:1,4; 23:11; Mk 9:34; Lk 9:46; 22:24,26), right up to the table at the Last Supper: "And there was also a strife among them, which of them should be accounted the greatest” (Lk 22:24 KJV).

22.x: “ye know what ye ask”: Jesus addresses the brothers directly, moving past the mother. He uses two metaphors for intense suffering: drinking from a bitter “cup” and being overwhelmed or submerged in a “baptism” of affliction. In their overconfident ambition, they quickly reply: “We are able.”

23.x: Jesus confirms they will indeed suffer for him, but explains that the ultimate seats of honor are distributed according to the Father’s sovereign design, not political lobbying. They must submit to the Father’s Will, just like the human Son does. James and John wanted the crown without the cross. Ironically, the two individuals who would eventually occupy the spaces on Jesus’ right and left hand during his earthly glorification were the two thieves crucified next to him. Furthermore, Jesus’ prophecy came true: James became the first apostle martyred (Acts 12:2), and John suffered lifelong persecution and exile on the island of Patmos (Rev 1:9).

The TR and MT include: “and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with” on both v22 & v23. However, the CT omits that part from both verses in order to follow the two oldest Greek manuscripts from Alexandria Egypt (Synaiticus & Vaticanus). Two possible solutions to this: (1) Some scribe knew this information from Mark 10:38-39, WHICH DOES NOT CONTAIN A VARIANT and reads as: “and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with” or perhaps from Luke’s account that does not have a variant either: “But I have a baptism to be baptized with” (Lk 12:50 KJV) and simply added it to Matthew so the people that only had access to Matthew’s gospel would have more complete information; (2) Matthew ALWAYS contained these words and Synaiticus & Vaticanus were faulty manuscripts that were never copied over nor preserved by the Church. I lean more towards option 2 since Vaticanus and Synaiticus overcorrect (they probably do correct sometimes when they reduce sentences that were probably expanded throughout the years, like “the King David” instead of simply “David”) and introduce errors and contradictions to Scripture (for example: “why callest thou me good? There is none good but one, that is, God,” which is found in multiple parallel passages: Mk 10:1-18; Mt 19:16-17; Lk 18:18-19; yet, in the CT, Matthew reads like: “Why do you ask me about WHAT IS GOO?” BSB).

24.x: The rest of the apostles (“the ten”) find out about this secret boardroom meeting and are instantly furious (“moved with indignation”) with James and John. However, the ten were not angry because they were holier or more humble than James and John; they were angry because the brothers beat them to the punch. Everyone in that circle was still competing for the top spot, exposing a deep rift of jealousy and political infighting among the disciples.

This exact moment in v.24 provides a massive historical and theological insight into how the disciples viewed church leadership at this point in time. In Catholicism, it is argued that back in Mt 16:18, Jesus had already established Peter as the “Rock,” effectively appointing him as the supreme leader, or the first Pope (Supreme Pontiff), over all the other apostles. However, the raw narrative of Matthew 20 completely uncercuts the idea that anyone in that group (including Jesus, Peter, or the other ten) recognized Peter as having a unique, supreme office. If James and John knew that Peter had already been designated by Jesus as the supreme earthly head of the kingdom, their request makes no sense. You do not ask to sit on the immediate right and left hand of the King if you already know that one of those seats is permanently locked down by Peter. They clearly believed the top spots were still wide open for anyone who could grab them. Verse 24 states that when the ten heard about it, they were collectively furious at the two brothers. If Peter was already recognized as the supreme ruler over the group, he wouldn’t have been part of a mutual, squabbling faction of ten equal men. He would have handled the situation as the commanding leader. Instead, the text treats the remaining ten as an equal group of peers who were all equally offended that two members of their EQUAL circle tried to elevate themselves. In the very next verses (25-28), Jesus has to step in to settle the dispute. Rather than saying: “Why are you guys arguing? I already told you Peter is in charge,” Jesus completely bans the concept of anyone exercising supreme hierarchical dominance over the others, saying: “Whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister.” At this crucial moment on the road to Jerusalem, the disciples did not see a hierarchy with Peter at the apex; they saw a brotherhood of equals, still clumsily wrestling with what true, servant-hearted leadership actually meant.

25.x: Jesus summons the twelve apostles closer. He points directly to the political structures they were all familiar with: the “princes of the Gentiles” (like the Roman emperors, Herodian kings, and governors). He notes that their style of leadership relies heavily on “exercising dominion” and “authority” upon the people beneath them. In the Greek text, the words used for “exercise dominion” (katakyrieuō) and “exercise authority” (katexousizō) carry a strong connotation of lording it over people or forcing them into submission. Jesus is saying: “You all know how the secular world works. It’s a top-down pyramid scheme. The people at the top use their power, titles, and muscle to push the people at the bottom around.” The disciples were angry because they wanted to be the ones at the top of that Roman-style pyramid.

26.x: Jesus draws a massive, unyielding line in the sand: “But it shall not be so among you.” He completely bans the top-down, authoritarian model of leadership within his community. He then redefines true greatness: if you want to be “great” (megas), your job description is to be a “minister.” The word “minister” here is the Greek word “diakonos”, which literally means a waiter, a servant, or someone who kicks up dust while running errands for others (the root of our modern word “deacon”). In the ancient world, being a table-waiter was considered lowly and completely devoid of honor. Jesus completely flips the script: in his kingdom, greatness is not measured by how many people serve you, but by how many people you actively serve.

27.x: Jesus takes the principle a step further, escalating the challenge. If being “great” means being a waiter, then wanting to be “chief” (the absolute first, or top leader) means you must become a “servant.” The word translated as “servant” here is much stronger than “diakonos,” it is the Greek word “doulos,” which literally means a bond-slave. A slave in Roman times had absolutely no legal rights, no personal agenda, and owned nothing; their entire existence was consumed with looking after the well-being and wishes of their master. If you wan tto move up in ranking (from “great” to “chief”), you must move down in posture (from a “table-waiter” to a “slave”). True leadership in Christ’s church is never about demanding titles, wearing crowns, or throwing weight around. The leader’s authority is earned through radical, low-level service to the family of God.

Compare Jesus’ teaching with that of the historical Roman Church. Verses 25-28 describe how Roman/Gentile rulers “lord it over” people through domination, hierarchy, and authoritarian control. Jesus then says “Not so with you” - establishing a radical contrast between earthly empire power and kingdom-of-God leadership. Catholic Rome (after the Church became the empire’s mandatory religion under Emperor Theodosius and later) adopted exactly the model Jesus condemned. When Jesus said: “Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion”, the Pope became a prince of the Church exercising dominion over all Europe. When Jesus said: “they that are great exercise authority upon them", Catholic hierarchy (Pope → cardinals → bishops) exercised authority upon all subjects. When Jesus said: “But it shall not be so among you”, Catholic Rome made Christianity MANDATORY BY IMPERIAL LAW: the exact “exercise dominion” Jesus forbade. The Catholic Church developed: (1) Papa Supremacy: the Pope as “Vicar of Christ” with authority over all bishops and believers; (2) Inquisition: using state power to force conformity; (3) Excommunication: political and spiritual domination; (4) Mandatory infant baptism: no voluntary choice; (5) State-enforced religion: dissent = treason (heresy laws). This is precisely what Jesus calls “princes of the Gentiles exercising dominion,” the opposite of “it shall not be so among you.” After 380AC (Edict of Thessalonica), Catholic Christianity became the only legal religion of the Roman Empire. All other religions (even other Christians) were banned or persecuted. Heretics were executed or exiled, and coercion replaced voluntary faith. Jesus in Mt 20:25-26 says: (1) Gentile rules exercise dominion (v.25); (2) “It shall not be so among you” (v.26) and (3) True greatness = being your minister/servant (v.26). Catholic Rome did the EXACT OPPOSITE: (1) The Pope and bishops exercised dominion over souls and states; (2) Used Imperial power to force submission; and (3) Made the faith mandatory through law rather than voluntary service. “Princes of the Gentile exercise dominion” (v.25): Pope became a prince with dominion over kingdoms. “It shall not be so among you” (v.26): Catholic Church became the prince exercising dominion. “Whosoever will be great… let him be your minister” (v.26): Pope claimed supreme authority over all bishops. “Nor that one should be your master” (v.27): Pope claimed to be amster of all (universal jurisdiction). “Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (v.28): Pope was served by all (gold, titles, obedience). Jessu’ Kingdom = servant leadership. Catholic Rome’s Church = imperial domination (the exact opposite).

28.x: Jesus connects his instruction directly to his own actions (“Even as..”). He uses his favorite messianic title: “Son of Man,” and explains that his mission on earth was completely the opposite of what people expected of a King. He didn’t come to be “ministered unto” (served), but “to minister” (to serve) and to give his life as a “random” for a multitude of people. If anyone had the right to demand a top-down, red-carpet, Roman-style royal treatment, it was Jesus. He is the creator of the universe wrapped in flesh. Yet, he utterly refused to elt people wait on him hand and foot. Instead, he spent his days healing the sick, feeding the hungry, washing dirty feet, and hanging out with society’s outcasts. He modeled the exact “waiter” (diakonos) lifestyle he just commanded his disciples to live. When Jesu came “to minister,” he shows that his entire earthly life was an act of service to humanity. He didn’t just come to die; he came to live an active life of love, showing us exactly what God’s character looks like in action. He redefines God not as a distant, demanding tyrant, but as a loving Father who steps down into our mess to help us. The phrase “to give his life a random for many” is incredibly important. In the ancient Greco-Roman world, a “random” (lytron) was the literal price paid to buy back a slave, a prisoner of war, or a captive to set them completely free. “For many” (anti pollōn): The Greek word “anti” literally means “in place of” or “as a substitute for.” Jesus is explicitly stating that humanity is held captive: trapped by sin, death, and brokenness. Because we couldn’t afford to pay the price to free ourselves. Jesus stepped up to pay it for us. His death on the cross wasn’t an accident or a political failure; it was a deliberate, substitutionary sacrifice. He traded his perfect life to buy our freedom. Think about how deeply this must have stung James, John, and the rest of the twelve. While they were busy bickering over who got to wear the biggest crown, Jesus was quietly preparing to pay the ultimate price on a cross. He proved that the only way to truly lead in his kingdom is to love people so much that you are willing to lay down your life for them.

29.x: Jesus and his disciples are passing through Jericho, an ancient oasis city located about 15 miles northeast of Jerusalem. Because Passover is just days away, a massive crowd (“great multitude”) of Jewish pilgrims is walking along with him, filling the narrow roads with noise, dust, and excitement. The setting is crucial. The atmosphere is loud and celebratory. Everyone is thinking about the upcoming festival and the potential political liberation of Israel. It is exactly the kind of environment where important religious teachers would ignore the lower classes of society to focus on the crowd or their own thoughts.

30.x: Two blind men are sitting down along the edge of the busy road. In the ancient world, blindness was an economic death sentence; without modern medical care or social systems, these men were entirely dependent on begging for survival. When they hear the roaring noise of the crowd and learn that “Jesus passed by,” they start screaming at the top of their lungs, using a specific title: “thou Son of David.” Notice what they call him. “Son of David” was a strictly Messianic title based on God’s promise to King David in 2 Samuel 7. Ironically, while the physically sighted religious leaders and disciples were spiritually blind to who Jesus really was, these two physically blind beggars had the spiritual sight to recognize him as the promised Messiah of Israel.

31.x: The traveling crowd (“multitude”) turns on the two men, scolding them (“rebuked them”) and telling them to shut up (“hold their peace”). Instead of silencing them, the opposition only fuels their desperation: they scream out even louder (“they cried the more”), repeating their plea for mercy. The crowd viewed these beggars as an annoying, low-status distraction to Jesus’ grand royal march into Jerusalem. This perfectly mirrors the human ambition Jesus just corrected in the previous verses. But the blind men knew this might be their only chance to ever meet the healer. Their relentless shouting is a raw expression of pure, unashamed faith.

32.x: Amidst the noise of thousands of people, Jesus hears the cry of the hurting.

33.x: Jesus stops dead in his tracks (“Jesus stood still”), commands that the men be brought to him, and asks a direct, simple question: “What will yet that I shall do unto you?” They reply instantly with their truest heart’s desire: “Lord, that our eyes may be opened.” This is a breathtaking display of servant-ministry. Jesus is on his way to save the world via the crucifixion, yet he has time to pause for two penniless outcasts. His question matches the exact phrasing he used with James and John in v.21(“What wilt thou?”). While the ambitious disciples asked for thrones of power, these humble beggars simply ask for their basic physical needs to be met so they can see.

34.x: Moved by deep, internal grief for their suffering (“had compassion”), Jesus reaches out and physically touches their sightless eyes. Instantly, their vision is completely restored. The verse ends with a beautiful detail: the moment they can see, they don’t run off to celebrate, they immediately join the crowd and “followed him.” Under the Old Covenant, touching something broken or diseased could make a person ritually unclean. But when Jesus touches brokenness, his power flows outward to heal it. By restoring their sight, Jesus performs a miracle that ancient Jewish prophecy explicitly tied to the arrival of the Messiah: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened” (Isa 35:5 KJV).

13-15.x: The master responds with perfect justice. He didn’t cheat the first group; he fulfilled his contract perfectly. He then asserts his right to be uniquely generous with his own wealth. The phrase “Is thine eye evil, because I am good?” (v.15) is an old idiom meaning “Are you jealous because I am generous” (this same Hebrew idiom is used in Mt 6:22-23, see notes there). This is the core theological climax of the parable. God’s grace operates on a completely different system than human economics. Justice means getting exactly what you earn. Grace means getting an unearned gift. The master shows that his kingdom is governed by radical generosity, and no one can dictate how God distributes His mercy.
